e.etymology: A form of Annabel, a medieval Scottish name that probably began as an alteration of Amabel, from Latin amabilis, lovable. The -belle spelling reads it as Anna plus French belle, beautiful.

assoc.t: haunted doll of the Annabelle and Conjuring horror films

e.note: Shares its name with the haunted doll of the Annabelle horror films (2014 onward).

e.meaning: pure (by long tradition; the true origin is debated)
e.etymology: From French Catherine and Greek Aikaterine, a name of debated origin. Early Christians tied it to Greek katharos, pure, which gave the th spelling. Saint Catherine of Alexandria spread it across Europe.
namesakes: Catherine the Great (empress of Russia)
Catherine, Princess of Wales (formerly Kate Middleton)
Catherine O'Hara (actress, Schitt's Creek and Home Alone)

e.etymology: A recent name that appears to build on amor, the Spanish, Portuguese and Latin word for love, with a feminine -a ending. In Portuguese amora is also the word for mulberry.

assoc.t: Amora the Enchantress, a Marvel Comics sorceress

e.etymology: A short form of Alexander, written the way it sounds, a variant of Xander. Alexander comes from Greek alexo, to defend, and aner, man.
A short form of Dorothea and Theodora, both built on Greek theos, god; on its own thea is the Greek word for goddess.
The feminine of Lucianus, a Roman name derived from Lucius, from Latin lux, light. It is used in Italian, Spanish and Portuguese.
A spelling of Carson, a Scottish surname of uncertain origin that became an American first name. The frontiersman Kit Carson is its best-known bearer.

e.meaning: I love you (the usual reading of the Zapotec source)
e.etymology: A Mexican name usually traced to the Zapotec phrase nadxieli, I love you, though the exact source is uncertain. It has been common in Mexico and among Hispanic families in the US since the 1990s.
From the name of the flower, Old English popaeg. It joined other flower names in Britain in the late 1800s and has been a favorite there since the 1990s.

assoc.t: poppy, the red flower whose seeds are used in baking
Queen Poppy, the pink heroine of the Trolls movies
red remembrance poppy worn for war dead

e.note: Poppy or Pop-Pop is what many American families call a grandfather.

e.meaning: from the alyssum flower, or a form of Alicia
e.etymology: A 20th-century name with more than one likely source: the alyssum flower, whose Greek name means against madness, and Alicia or Elissa. It was among the most popular US girls' names around 2000.
namesakes: Alyssa Milano (actress, Who's the Boss? and Charmed)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jayden, coined by American parents in the late 20th century by putting J in front of the sound of Aidan, Braden and Hayden. It also resembles the rare biblical name Jadon.
namesakes: Jaden Smith (actor and musician, son of Will Smith)

e.etymology: An Italian pet form of Antonia, the feminine of Antonio, from the Roman family name Antonius, whose meaning is unknown. It has spread through Latin America and into the US.
The feminine of Camillus, a Roman family name and a term for a youth who served at religious rites, probably of Etruscan origin. In Virgil's Aeneid Camilla is a swift warrior maiden.
namesakes: Queen Camilla (wife of King Charles III)

assoc.t: Queen Camilla, wife of King Charles III

e.etymology: A pet form of Archibald, from Germanic words meaning genuine and bold, long a favorite in Scotland. It has been given as a full name since the 1800s.
namesakes: Prince Archie of Sussex (son of Prince Harry and Meghan)
Archie Bunker (All in the Family)
Archie Manning (NFL quarterback, father of Peyton and Eli)

assoc.t: red-haired teen of Archie Comics and Riverdale
Prince Archie, son of Prince Harry and Meghan

e.etymology: From the English word for the season, also an old surname. It has been a girls' name in the US mainly since the 2000s.
namesakes: Winter (dolphin with a prosthetic tail in the film Dolphin Tale)

e.etymology: From Old French esmé, esteemed, close in form to aimé, loved. It began as a man's name in 16th-century Scotland with Esmé Stewart, Duke of Lennox, and is now given mostly to girls.
namesakes: Esme Cullen (vampire matriarch in Twilight)

assoc.t: Esme Cullen, the vampire mother in Twilight

e.etymology: From the Colorado city, named in 1858 for territorial governor James W. Denver. His surname comes from an English place name, probably Old English for the Danes' crossing.

assoc.t: capital of Colorado, the Mile High City
singer John Denver

e.etymology: The feminine of Adrian, from Latin Hadrianus, a man from Hadria, a town in northern Italy that also gave its name to the Adriatic Sea.
namesakes: Adriana Lima (Brazilian supermodel)

e.meaning: dweller by a riverbank or hillside
e.etymology: From an English surname for someone who lived beside a bank, a slope or the edge of a river. As a first name it is a 21st-century arrival alongside Brooks and Hayes.

assoc.t: banks, as in financial institutions and money
model and TV host Tyra Banks
the Banks family of Mary Poppins

e.etymology: A spelling of Cade, an English surname with several medieval sources, among them an Old English personal name Cada and a word for a cask. It is also a short form of Kaden.
From a northern English surname for someone who lived near a bridge, from Middle English brigge. It has been used as an American first name mainly since the 2010s.
From the English word son with a -y ending, long an affectionate way to address a boy. Italian American families also used it as a nickname for Santino and Salvatore.
namesakes: Sonny Bono (singer of Sonny and Cher, later a congressman)
Sonny Corleone (eldest son in The Godfather)
Sonny Rollins (jazz saxophonist)
e.note: Sounds the same as sunny, so the spelling will often need to be given.

assoc.t: Sonny Bono of the duo Sonny & Cher

e.etymology: The Italian feminine of Alessio, from the Greek name Alexios, built on alexo, to defend. It is the Italian counterpart of Alexis and Alexia.
namesakes: Alessia Cara (Grammy-winning Canadian singer)

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Maya or Maia, names with several unrelated sources, among them the Greek goddess Maia. The spelling took off around 2000 with the R&B singer Mya.

assoc.t: Mya, R&B singer of Case of the Ex

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins Dax to the -ton ending of Paxton, Jaxton and Braxton.

e.meaning: one who grinds grain at a mill
e.etymology: From the English and Scottish occupational surname for a miller. It is one of the most common American surnames and a recent arrival as a first name.

assoc.t: Miller beer, as in Miller Lite and High Life

e.etymology: The French feminine of Nicolas, from Greek Nikolaos, built on nike, victory, and laos, people. It was one of the most popular US girls' names of the 1970s and 1980s.
namesakes: Nicole Kidman (Oscar-winning actress)
Nicole Richie (TV personality and designer)
Nicole Scherzinger (singer, The Pussycat Dolls)

e.etymology: From an English surname, a variant of Page, the title of a young servant or attendant in a noble household. It became a girls' name in the US in the 20th century.
namesakes: Paige Bueckers (UConn and WNBA basketball star)

e.etymology: The English word, used as an aspirational name in the US since the 2010s. It rose after Rob Kardashian and Blac Chyna named their daughter Dream in 2016.
namesakes: Dream Kardashian (daughter of Rob Kardashian and Blac Chyna)

assoc.t: Dream, a masked Minecraft YouTuber
Dream, lead of Neil Gaiman's The Sandman

e.meaning: of the Julius family; also Julie plus Anna
e.etymology: A spelling of Juliana, the feminine of the Roman name Julianus, from Julius. In English it is often treated as a blend of Julie and Anna.
namesakes: Julianna Margulies (actress, ER and The Good Wife)

e.meaning: the Holy Trinity; three in one
e.etymology: From the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, from Latin trinitas, threefold. In use as a name since the 1970s, it surged after the character Trinity appeared in The Matrix in 1999.
namesakes: Trinity Rodman (US soccer star, daughter of Dennis Rodman)

assoc.t: Trinity, the hacker heroine of The Matrix
Trinity, the first atomic bomb test in 1945

e.etymology: From the Irish surname Mac Cionaoith, son of Cionaodh, an old Gaelic personal name. It became an American girls' name in the 1990s alongside Mackenzie.
namesakes: Mckenna Grace (actress, Gifted and Ghostbusters: Afterlife)
